body.text: On November 19, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung appealed to leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit to back efforts to restart talks with North Korea. He called peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula essential to shared prosperity among the 21 economies of the forum.

“I ask for your active interest and cooperation in this effort,” Lee said during his remarks on Thursday, while expressing his hope for a resumption of dialogue with Pyongyang that could lead to talks on ending the war on the peninsula and building a lasting peace regime.
A day earlier, Lee had delivered a similar message to Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen during their bilateral summit meeting.

“Peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula are in the common interests of both countries,” Lee told Xi in his opening remarks at the summit. Lee expressed hope that the two countries could work together toward an era of peaceful coexistence on the peninsula. According to National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac, Lee asked Xi to play a constructive role on issues concerning the Korean Peninsula. Xi lent support to efforts to ease tensions on the peninsula and to dialogue between North Korea and the United States, Wi added.

On November 17, Lee had held talks on regional security with Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae on the sidelines of a gathering of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila. That bilateral sit-down came six months after Takaichi visited Lee’s hometown of Andong, South Korea, as a follow-up on the so-called shuttle diplomacy.

The presidential house of South Korea said the two leaders noted increasingly active discussions among major powers on peace and stability in Northeast Asia. They agreed that strategic communication between their countries is more important than ever.

Surprisingly, Lee also spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin for about 10 minutes on November 18 after the two crossed paths at a banquet hosted by Xi. Relations between Seoul and Moscow have worsened since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Russia in 2022, and the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia has added to the strain. Issues concerning the two Koreas and the North Korean nuclear program were raised but not discussed at length, according to the South’s local news media reports.
Based on public readouts released thus far, the Korean Peninsula was not a major topic at the trilateral summit also held on November 19 among the United States, China, and Russia.

In recent weeks, North Korea has not responded positively to Seoul’s request for dialogue. South Korea has proposed military talks since November 2025. Seoul repeated the offer on October 23 to confirm where the Military Demarcation Line lies and to prevent accidental clashes along the border. A mine explosion in the Demilitarized Zone along that border on September 21 had injured South Korean troops. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea, has denied any responsibility while reaffirming plans to keep fortifying the border and describing the South as a hostile state.

With Pyongyang closed to talks, Seoul has turned to Beijing and Moscow for support. In May 2022, China and Russia vetoed a resolution drafted by the United States to tighten sanctions on North Korea at the United Nations Security Council. In fact, amid tightening ties, both Beijing and Moscow have seemingly dropped any policy of denuclearization. Recent diplomatic trends give the two countries little reason to press Pyongyang on behalf of Seoul, implying that measures to punish North Korea’s growing nuclear arsenal at the UNSC are no longer feasible.

So far Xi and Putin have offered words of support for easing tensions but no publicly reported steps to bring Pyongyang to the table. And, under the current circumstances, it is unrealistic to expect either Xi or Putin would pressure Kim to negotiate with Trump as the trilateral cooperation between China, Russia and North Korea has been fruitful.

Earlier in the year, Trump had expressed his desire to hold another summit with Kim Jong Un, and speculation centered on the APEC summit in Shenzhen. However, North Korea has shown little interest. As of writing, there have been no signs of Kim moving to China for a meeting with Trump. Instead, the North’s state-controlled media reported on Kim overseeing regions in North Korea in the past few days.

In this context, Lee’s “END” initiative on North Korea may need to be recalibrated. Without engagement by China and Russia, South Korea cannot fully resolve the growing nuclear threats of North Korea. However, Seoul’s hands seem to have been tied by other security challenges, including the aggravated power competition between the United States and China, the ongoing Ukraine War, and the Israel-Iran-U.S. war. In light of this, South Korea needs to come up with a bipartisan policy on North Korea that can last despite external conditions.
